https://www.dw.com/en/eurovision-bars-co.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IiJH This year’s Eurovision Song Contest was won by Bulgaria’s entrant Dara, who won with her song "Bangaranga," meaning the 2027 contest will take place in the country for the first time Image: Georg Hochmuth/APA/AFP Advertisement Eurovision Song Contest organizers announced rule changes that would prevent countries involved in an armed conflict from hosting the event. Israel and Ukraine are among the countries the rule could affect, with both having enjoyed recent success in the competition. What did the Eurovision organizers say? Eurovision is typically staged by the broadcaster from the country that won the previous edition as part of a co-production involving members of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU). Under the new rules, "the winning broadcaster will automatically be ineligible to host the Contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region," the EBU said. Canada to join 2027 Eurovision Song Contest To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The EBU may commission an independent security assessment if necessary. If the winning broadcaster is deemed unable to stage the contest, another broadcaster will be selected. Why is the Eurovision changing the rules? The EBU did not name any particular country as the reason, but Israel finished second at Eurovision in both 2025 and 2026. Five countries — Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Iceland — boycotted the 2026 contest in Vienna, saying they could not participate alongside Israel because of the war in Gaza . Israel is currently involved in the war in Iran. The new rule formalizes a challenge Eurovision has faced before. Ukraine hosted the contest in 2017 despite fighting in the east of the country, but after winning Eurovision in 2022 it was unable to stage the following year's event because of Russia's full-scale invasion. Liverpool instead hosted Eurovision 2023 in the United Kingdom on Ukraine's behalf. Russia has been excluded from Eurovision since 2022, when the EBU banned it following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. What else is changing about the Eurovision? Under the new rules, the EBU is raising the minimum age for performers from 16 to 18 to reduce pressure on young artists. Lead vocals must also be performed live and cannot be supported by pre-recorded voices. Russia launches Eurovision rival music contest after ban To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The EBU said the clarification was intended to protect the integrity of performances and ensure audiences hear the lead singer live. Eurovision director Martin Green said the contest's rules were reviewed each year to keep the competition fair and transparent. Next year's contest will be held in Bulgaria following Bulgarian pop singer Dara's victory in Eurovision 2026 in Vienna with "Bangaranga." Beállítom Ruszin-Szendi Romulusz honvédelmi miniszter hétfő délután Szolnokról jelentkezett be , miután lezuhant a Magyar Honvédség egyik Gripen vadászgépe . A miniszter közölte, hogy a pilóta jól van, és már átszállították a budapesti Honvéd Kórházba. Ruszin-Szendi megkérte a mellette álló vezérezredest, hogy számoljon be az ügy fejleményeiről. A gép veszélyjelzést adott le, a kísérő megpróbálta a gépet bekísérni a repülőtérre, a műszerezettsége eltűnt a fedélzetről. Ez a megoldás a leszállásig működött, de akkor a gép olyan manőverbe kezdett a földön, ami után a pilóta úgy döntött, hogy katapultálnia kell. A Gripen a katapultálás után balra kisodródott, megállt, majd kigyulladt. A vezérezredes szerint a pilótának sikerült elkerülnie, hogy ezt a manővert ne lakott területen kelljen végrehajtania. Azt mondta, az utolsó pillanatig próbálta irányítani az elektronikával már nem rendelkező gépet. Megjegyezte, hogy a tűzoltók 5 perc alatt a helyszínen voltak, és megkezdték az oltást, így pedig elkerülték, hogy nagyobb kár keletkezzen a repülőtéren. Majd egy tábornok arról beszélt, hogy a vadászgépek légvédelmi készültségben voltak. Közölte, hogy ezeknek a gépeknek minden nap fel kell szállniuk és légi harcot kell vívniuk egymással. Egy-egy elleni légi harc közben érkezett egy olyan hibajelzés a gép fedélzetéről, amiért meg kellett szakítani a gyakorlást. Ekkor már tudni lehetett, hogy nem tudnak elrepülni Kecskemétig, ezért döntöttek a szolnoki leszállás mellett. A bejövetel utolsó szakaszában történt az esemény, amely miatt katapultálnia kellett a pilótának. Ruszin-Szendi azt is elmondta, hogy a gépen levegő-levegő rakéták és gépágyúlőszerek is voltak. Szerinte ha a tűzoltók nem végezték volna hatékonyan a munkájukat, akkor nagyobb baj is történhetett volna. Hozzátette, hogy a feketedoboz kiértékelése még hátra van, és a további fejleményekről is be fognak számolni. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Photograph: Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA via AP US-Israel war on Iran US launches new airstrikes on Iranian targets as hostilities flare Move from Washington quashes hopes that exchange of fire last weekend might not presage ⁠wider renewal of hostilities Middle East crisis live – latest updates Reuters Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.03 EDT First published on Tue 1 Sep 2026 13.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US launched new airstrikes on Iranian targets on Tuesday, quashing hopes that an exchange of fire last ⁠weekend might not presage a ⁠wider renewal of hostilities. Oil prices had ​already risen after that first exchange of direct attacks since July and after reports of two tankers being hit leaving the strait of Hormuz, the global oil supply waterway that Iran has effectively closed to shipping. Tehran remained defiant, warning ⁠that it would prevent oil being exported from the Gulf, despite a threat by Donald Trump to hit Iran “hard” in response to the renewed Iranian strikes, and a warning from Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, that Washington was about to ⁠impose new sanctions. “Today at 12 p.m. ET (1600 GMT), U.S. forces began striking Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran,” US Central Command posted on X. “The strikes follow ​recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of ‌Hormuz and against American service members deployed to ‌the region.” Iran’s state broadcaster said there had been reports of explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island, on the northern side of the strait. The state-linked news agency Nour ‌News said there had been reports of explosions in the port city of Bandar Abbas and in Chabahar, a port on the southern coast. The six-month conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before the weekend strikes, in which US forces attacked Iran’s Larak Island on Sunday and Iran responded by launching missiles at two US airbases in Jordan. Although he warned of a US response to the Iranian strikes, the US president also told reporters on Monday that they did not signal a return to full-scale war, and a senior Iranian source told Reuters they were a “limited ‌and contained confrontation”. However, Trump made dire threats against Tehran on social media. He warned that if Iran retaliates against the US’s latest strikes, “they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran”. The ominous last part of Trump’s message was starkly reminiscent of threats the US president has made in the past that could amount to war crimes if carried out, including threatening to destroy critical civilian infrastructure such as power plants and bridges, threatening to bomb Iran “ back to the Stone Ages ”, and an April threat that “ a whole civilization will die tonight ” if a peace deal wasn’t reached. In Iran, the Fars news agency quoted an IRGC spokesperson as saying the US “will regret its new attacks”. More recently pledges by both sides to respond to further attacks have highlighted how quickly a conflict that has increasingly been fought through sanctions, blockades and economic pressure could spill back into military action. Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, had said early on Tuesday ​that Tehran would reciprocate immediately if Washington honoured its commitments under a June memorandum of understanding (MOU) that was intended to halt the conflict. The MOU declared an end to fighting that has now killed thousands in Iran and Lebanon since US and Israeli strikes began on 28 February. But it also deferred many of the most difficult issues and paved the way for a broader 60-day negotiation period – which passed without further agreement. “I am stating clearly that if the US returns to its commitments under the ⁠memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Pezeshkian said in the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, at ​a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, which includes Russia ​and China. But Iranian officials have shown no public ​sign of bowing to pressure. “If the enemy wants us not to export oil from the Persian Gulf, no one will be ​able to export oil,” Mohammad Baqer QalibafIran’s parliament speaker was ​quoted as saying by Iranian media. If ​the US intensified its “siege”, he said Tehran would respond militarily. Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, told a press conference in Tehran that Washington was “addicted to making excessive demands and has mistaken negotiations for dictating terms”. “As long as they act in this manner, they will certainly get no result other than what they have achieved so far,” he added, warning that Tehran would “use all our capabilities, whether on the battlefield or through our diplomatic apparatus”. https://www.thewestmorlandgazette.co.uk/.text: Leisure Travel 11 autumn walking breaks from Manchester Airport from £31 Leisure Travel By Imogen Barber Reporter Share 0 Comments 4 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. While the Lake District and Peak District offer plenty of spectacular scenery closer to home, direct flights from Manchester Airport can take walkers to autumn landscapes much further afield. From Ireland's mountains and Italy's lakes to the forests of Canada and the Great Wall of China, here are 11 destinations suggested for an autumn walking break. 1. Nízke Tatry National Park, Slovakia Flights: Manchester to Bratislava with Ryanair, from £33pp return. Slovakia's Tatra Mountains are a long-established hiking destination, with vast beech and spruce forests turning shades of gold and orange during October. Tatras Mountains in Autumn. (Image: Maciek Sulkowski via Unsplash.com) Walkers can explore routes around Chopok, Ďumbier and the Demänovská Valley, with panoramic views across the surrounding countryside. After a day on the trails, visitors can also try traditional Slovak dishes including kapustnica soup and sheep's cheese dumplings. 2. Red Wine Hiking Trail, Germany Flights: Manchester to Cologne with Ryanair, from £65pp return. Germany's famous Rotweinwanderweg , or Red Wine Hiking Trail, runs through the Ahr Valley, south of Cologne. The route links a string of wine villages and passes through vineyards which take on deep red and gold colours during autumn. As its name suggests, the trail also provides plenty of opportunities to stop and sample some of the area's local wines. 3. Stockholm, Sweden Flights: Manchester to Stockholm with Scandinavian Airlines, from £150pp return. Stockholm offers the chance to combine a city break with walks through classic Scandinavian autumn scenery. Forests of birch, aspen and pine surround lakes and islands, while trails through Tyresta National Park and around Lake Mälaren provide opportunities to see Sweden's seasonal colours. Tyresta also has a 5km 'stroller loop', making it an option for families with younger children. 4. Scottish Highlands Flights: Manchester to Aberdeen with Loganair, from £211pp return. Autumn brings fewer crowds to the Scottish Highlands, while forests of Scots pine and native birch take on shades of gold and copper. The Cairngorms offer numerous walking routes with views across mountains, forests and lochs. Those travelling through Aberdeen can also round off a day outdoors with a dram of Scottish whisky. 5. Kerry Mountains, Ireland Flights: Manchester to Kerry with Ryanair, from £31pp return. The landscape surrounding Killarney National Park turns colourful during the autumn months. Popular walking areas include Torc Mountain and the Gap of Dunloe, while experienced hikers can tackle Carrauntoohil, Ireland's highest mountain. Killarney itself provides a convenient base for exploring the national park and sits on the shores of Lough Leane. 6. Lake Iseo, Italy Flights: Manchester to Milan Bergamo with Ryanair, from £31pp return. Italy's lakes are well known for their mountain scenery, and autumn brings another dimension as the wooded hillsides change colour. Lake Iseo is also home to Monte Isola, a large island in the middle of the lake with villages and a network of picturesque walking routes. Cars are not permitted on the island, helping to create a quieter setting for an autumn break. 7. Julian Alps and Lake Bled, Slovenia Flights: Manchester to Ljubljana with easyJet, from £60pp return. Lake Bled is one of Slovenia's best-known sights, surrounded by forests which take on their autumn colours around October. Bled Castle over Lake Bled, Slovenia, in Autumn. (Image: Pixabay) Travellers can head beyond the lake into the Julian Alps, where walking routes run through alpine woodland and mountain valleys. Nearby Triglav is Slovenia's highest mountain and an important national symbol, appearing on the country's coat of arms and flag. 8. Ontario, Canada Flights: Manchester to Toronto with Air Transat, from £419pp return. Ontario is renowned for its autumn colours, particularly the vivid reds associated with its maple trees. Algonquin Provincial Park and the Niagara Escarpment are among the options for walkers looking to venture beyond Toronto. Autumn in Algonquin Provincial Park, Ontario, Canada. (Image: Pixabay) Visitors staying in the city can also experience autumn scenery at Rouge National Urban Park. 9. North-East USA Flights: Manchester to New York JFK with Virgin Atlantic, from £718pp return. New York can serve as a starting point for exploring some of the north-eastern United States' famous autumn landscapes. The Hudson Valley, Catskills and Adirondacks offer forests filled with reds, oranges and browns. Those travelling further into New England could also explore the White Mountains in New Hampshire and the scenery surrounding the Kancamagus Highway. 10. Northern Pakistan Flights: Manchester to Islamabad with Pakistan International Airlines, from £822pp return. Northern Pakistan offers a dramatically different setting for an autumn walking holiday. Around Hunza and Skardu, poplar and apricot trees turn vivid shades of gold, contrasting with the towering mountain landscapes of the region. The valleys surrounding the Karakoram provide some of the most dramatic scenery on the list. 11. Beijing area, China Flights: Manchester to Beijing with Hainan Airlines, from £535pp return. Autumn provides walkers with the opportunity to explore the countryside surrounding Beijing in cooler conditions. Several sections of the Great Wall pass through forested mountains where leaves can turn shades of red and yellow. The surrounding hills and mountains provide further walking opportunities and sweeping views across northern China's landscape. The cheapest options For travellers looking primarily at price, the lowest return fares supplied are £31pp to Kerry and Milan Bergamo, followed by £33pp to Bratislava.
